lines.text: A Bloom filter answers a single question about a key: either maybe present, or definitely absent.
For a key that was genuinely inserted earlier, could it ever come back definitely absent?
No, never, genuinely.
At any budget at all, an inserted key always comes back as at least maybe present.
Run it for real: at every single bits-per-key budget tried, every key that was actually inserted genuinely came back possibly present, with not one false negative anywhere.
Build that same filter again, but with a much tighter bits-per-key budget this time.
Does a key that was never inserted at all ever come back maybe present?
Yes, genuinely, sometimes.
Some keys that were never inserted do come back as maybe present.
Run it for real: that tight bits-per-key budget genuinely produced real false positives, against keys that had never been inserted at all.
Spend far more bits per key on that exact same filter instead.
Does that genuinely change how often a never-inserted key comes back maybe present?
Yes, genuinely, it drops.
Spending more bits per key lowers how often that happens.
Run it for real: spending far more bits per key genuinely lowered the measured false-positive rate on that same filter, by a wide margin.
One real production system states an actual bits-per-key table directly, in its own documentation.
Does a small increase near the low end of that table buy as much improvement as the same size increase further up it?
No, genuinely.
The low end of that table buys far more improvement for every bit spent than the same increase further up does.
That system's own numbers state it directly: spending a small amount near the low end of the table buys far more improvement, per bit, than spending that same amount further up it.
That same system's own documentation also states, directly, why any of this spending is worth doing at all.
A filter like this one can cut the number of unneeded disk reads a lookup would otherwise have to pay for, substantially, often by close to two orders of magnitude.

lines.text: So here's the shape of this whole topic: a filter like this one never forgets a key it was actually given, so when it says a key is absent, that's genuine proof, not a guess.
A positive answer is the opposite: it only grants permission to go check further, since it can occasionally be wrong about a key that was never there at all.
Spending more bits per key on that filter genuinely buys a lower rate of those wrong answers, though with real diminishing returns.
The entire reason any of this is worth doing is that it lets a lookup skip opening most of the files it would otherwise have had to check.
